hints: Look carefully at the condensed formula and redraw it as a full structure, spotting where the triple and double bonds must be.
Remember that every single bond is one sigma, a double bond is one sigma plus one pi, and a triple bond is one sigma plus two pi.
Count all C-H sigma bonds plus all C-C sigma bonds separately, then add the pi bonds from the multiple bonds to finish the total.
walkthrough:
**Draw Out The Real Structure**

Great start, let's turn that shorthand into something we can see. The formula becomes $\text{HC}\equiv\text{C-CH}_2\text{-CH}_2\text{-CH=C(CH}_3)_2$.

So we have one triple bond at the left end and one double bond near the right end.

**Count The Pi Bonds First**

This is the easy part. A triple bond $\text{C}\equiv\text{C}$ contains $2\pi$ bonds, and a double bond $\text{C=C}$ contains $1\pi$ bond.

$$ \text{total } \pi = 2 + 1 = 3 $$

**Count All The Sigma Bonds**

Now count every single sigma link. First, count C-H bonds. There are $1+2+2+1+6 = 12$ hydrogens, so $12\sigma$ from C-H.

Next, count C-C sigma links. There are 7 C-C connections, each gives $1\sigma$:
$$ \text{total } \sigma = 12 \text{ (C-H)} + 7 \text{ (C-C)} = 19 $$

**Put It Together**

We have $19\sigma$ bonds and $3\pi$ bonds in total. That matches $19\sigma$ $3\pi$ perfectly.

options.A: Incorrect. $17\sigma$ is too low because two sigma bonds have been missed, often the C-C sigma bonds inside the triple and double bonds are forgotten.
options.B: Incorrect. $17\sigma$ $5\pi$ miscounts both types. $5\pi$ would mean far more multiple bonds than the one triple ($2\pi$) plus one double ($1\pi$) actually present.
options.C: Incorrect. $18\sigma$ $4\pi$ is close but off by one in each. It suggests an extra pi bond and a missing C-H or C-C sigma, a common slip when the two $\text{CH}_3$ groups are not fully counted.
options.D: Correct. There are 12 C-H sigma + 7 C-C sigma = $19\sigma$, plus $2\pi$ from the $\text{C}\equiv\text{C}$ and $1\pi$ from the $\text{C=C}$, giving $3\pi$ total.
